canon.heading: Make the association easy to carry.
canon.standfirst: Read Chapter 16, "Positioning an Island: Jamaica," from Al Ries and Jack Trout's Positioning on PDF pages 248-255. Study how a place can narrow its story to a memorable association and use that frame to organize choice.
canon.readerIntro: Read this chapter as a positioning exercise. Mark the association Jamaica is trying to own, the alternatives it makes less relevant, and the details that make the position believable. Then audit one brand or place: name its current frame, the frame it should reject, and one proof point that would make the sharper position easier to choose. Stop at PDF page 255.

blocks.label: 01 / Name the association
paragraphs: Positioning begins by choosing the mental association a subject wants to make easiest to retrieve.
Mark the phrase or image that gives the place a memorable handle rather than a catalogue of attributes.

blocks.label: 02 / Notice the tradeoff
paragraphs: A sharp position gains force by making some claims less central. Notice what the chosen frame excludes and why that sacrifice improves memorability.
Ask which competing interpretation the position is designed to displace.

blocks.label: 03 / Connect frame to proof
paragraphs: The association has to be supported by details people can recognize, not merely repeated as a slogan.
Underline the evidence that makes the intended frame feel like a credible expectation.

blocks.label: 04 / Audit one position
paragraphs: Choose one brand, destination, or product that currently tries to stand for too many things.
Rewrite its position as one association, one rejected frame, and one proof point.

closeReading: What single association is Jamaica being asked to own?
What does the chosen frame make less relevant or exclude?
Which details turn the position from a slogan into a believable expectation?
Choose one brand or place. What frame does it currently own, and which competing frame should it reject?
What proof point would make the sharper position easier to remember and choose?

principle.heading: Let one place stand for one idea.
principle.body: A memorable position is a shortcut through a crowded category: one association, a clear contrast, and enough proof to make the association credible.
principle.example: A destination does not need to claim every attractive quality. It can own one travel expectation and let the name, itinerary, imagery, and proof reinforce that expectation.
principle.practice: Take one brand or place and write three lines: the association to own, the competing frame to reject, and the proof that should make the association credible.

output.heading: Make the position retrievable.
output.body: The strongest frame is narrow enough to remember and useful enough to guide the next choice.

signals.heading: Five current signals on making a position clear enough to choose.

fieldNotes.title: OpenAI gives sales teams one job-shaped starting point
fieldNotes.whatHappened: OpenAI introduced ChatGPT for Sales, including a Sales plugin and more than 30 new or expanded partner plugins for account selection, call preparation, tailored proposals, follow-up, and pipeline risk.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: The offer is framed around a recognizable job—shortening the sales cycle—rather than asking buyers to remember a long list of AI capabilities. A narrow job makes the product easier to place in an existing workflow.
fieldNotes.watch: When evaluating an AI product, ask whether its first screen names the job it owns and the next action it helps someone take, or merely repeats the category label.

fieldNotes.title: Meta puts a personal AI agent in a new market
fieldNotes.whatHappened: Meta made Muse available in Australia and described it as a personal AI agent built for everyone, extending the app beyond a feature announcement into a distinct consumer proposition.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: The label does positioning work before the feature list begins: personal, agentic, and broadly accessible. The promise will be credible only if the first interactions make the user's own context and intent feel central.
fieldNotes.watch: Track the first repeatable behavior Muse creates—creation, conversation, or task completion—and whether users can explain the difference from a general chatbot after one session.

fieldNotes.title: Apple tests whether health AI can earn trust through evidence
fieldNotes.whatHappened: Apple launched a research study exploring how AI could help people understand health information and prepare for conversations with clinicians, using participant data and feedback to evaluate the experience.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: In a high-trust category, the position cannot be only 'AI for health.' The study frames the useful role more narrowly—as preparation and understanding—while evidence and clinical context supply the proof.
fieldNotes.watch: Separate the promised association from the proof system behind it: who validates the output, what uncertainty is shown, and whether the product helps a person take a safer next step.

fieldNotes.title: Shopify says the commerce shelf is becoming an agentic recommendation layer
fieldNotes.whatHappened: Shopify reported that AI-driven traffic to its stores grew 2.6x year over year and AI-referred orders grew 3.3x; it said about 75% of AI-referred purchases came from outside the top 100 product categories.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: Discovery is shifting from owning a visible shelf to being legible to the system making the recommendation. A product's use case, difference, and proof need to survive an agent's interpretation, not just a storefront visit.
fieldNotes.watch: Audit whether product data states the intended occasion and fit clearly enough for an agent to recommend the item beyond the obvious category shortlist.

tweets.author: Palmer Luckey
tweets.title: A founder rejects the consensus frame for his next product
tweets.summary: Luckey says SLAB is an older seastead project rather than the AI datacenter story attached to it. The fragment is useful as a positioning example: he is fighting to choose the frame people carry forward, even when the more current category would be easier to repeat.
tweets.text:
Selling Oculus to Facebook in 2014 gave me money for helicopter flight lessons and developing a seastead called SLAB with a 1,000 year design life.

The goal was to be cheaper than land and absent state/local laws that cripple critical American industries like metal processing, medical research/treatment, desalination, oil refining, chemical engineering, and more. Me and a few close friends cashed it up at a $1B valuation back in 2017, and while it still has a long way to go, there has been significant progress towards my goal of reviving manifest destiny and westward expansion. At a time when most of the seasteading community wanted to escape the US and smoke pot, this was the one project explicitly designed to make America stronger, a relief valve for ill considered or outdated rules and regulations.

I am only talking about it now because a few media outlets got wind of me and some friends topping up the coffers and plan on calling SLAB my new floating AI datacenter project. It is way cooler than that, way older than that, and I hate looking like a hype-chasing consensus loser, so now you have to read this tweet.
